newsitem.title: NORWAY: East Timor activist shares peace prize.
newsitem.headline: East Timor activist shares peace prize.

text.p: The award of the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize to East Timor resistance leader Jose Ramos Horta and Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo recognises two men who dedicated themselves in different ways to finding peace in their homeland.

Ramos Horta is the driving force behind and spokesman for Fretilin, the main East Timorese group which resisted Jakarta's rule after Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony in 1975. Indonesia later annexed East Timor.
The Indonesian government condemned the inclusion of Ramos Horta in the prize.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee said it had made the award to the two men "for their work toward a just and peaceful solution to the conflict in East Timor."
Ramos Horta recognised the differences between him and Belo.

"The resistance has a special agenda, the church has a different one. But there is one common goal -- peace, freedom and dignity," the bearded 48-year-old said told a news conference on the eve of Tuesday's award ceremony in Oslo.
"We are willing, open to engage in a dialogue with Indonesia without preconditions, in the framework of the United Nations in thre search of a solution to the problems of East Timor," he said.
Ramos Horta fled East Timor three days before the Indonesian invasion in December 1975. He now lives in Sydney but campaigns around the world for independence for East Timor.

"I receive the news with pleasure and with sadness," he said in a radio interview after the award was announced in October. He said Fretilin's military leader Xanana Gusmao, who is serving a 20-year prison sentence in Jakarta, should have been awarded the prize.
Even before Indonesia's occupation, Ramos Horta had advocated East Timorese independence and in 1970 was exiled to Mozambique for two years by the Lisbon authorities for his activities.
Three of his brothers and a sister died after Indonesian troops invaded the predominantly Roman Catholic territory 2,000 km (1,200 miles) east of Jakarta.
He was then acting as secretary for foreign affairs and information for Fretilin, the Revolutionary Front for the Liberation of East Timor, the main group seeking Timorese independence.
The United Nations has refused to recognise Indonesia's annexation of the territory and still regards Portugal as the administering power.
